einzeiler: How leaders build collective identity and active listening with Vanessa Beasley
kurzfassung: Adam Grant speaks with Trinity University president and rhetoric expert Vanessa Beasley about how leaders construct collective identity. They explore the evolution of presidential rhetoric, the importance of acknowledging shared problems before offering solutions, and why learning to listen is a vital leadership skill. The conversation also covers reimagining higher education, the leader attribution error, and the challenges of student engagement during commencement speeches.
stichpunkte: Vanessa Beasley explains that early U.S. presidents rhetorically created the concept of the American people through foundational addresses like inaugural speeches.
Effective leadership communication requires acknowledging a shared problem or threat before introducing novel solutions.
Leaders frequently commit the leader attribution error by taking sole credit for an organization's success, which diminishes citizen and employee agency.
The us-versus-them narrative is a powerful identity-building tool, but it carries significant risks when the perceived enemy becomes overly threatening.
Trinity University shifted from a respected regional institution to a major national liberal arts college by leaning into undergraduate business and engineering programs.
Vanessa Beasley teaches a dedicated university class on listening to help students develop a non-reactive, non-anxious presence.
Commencement speech disruptions reflect modern social media habits of immediate thumbs-up or thumbs-down reactions rather than thoughtful processing.
Intensive, immersive teaching formats create higher psychological safety and accountability, resulting in deeper student learning.

clips.hook: No conception of an American people before national news and telegraphs
clips.text: Prior to widespread postal and telegraph networks, citizens felt local rather than national ties, meaning the concept of a unified American people was constructed over time through presidential rhetoric.

clips.hook: Solution aversion: denying problems when you dislike the fix
clips.text: When people reject a leader's proposed solution, their initial psychological impulse is to deny that the underlying problem even exists.
Active listening is about valuing another person and seeking to understand their perspective even when you are certain you will never agree with them.

clips.hook: The worst leadership advice: Just be yourself
clips.text: Telling leaders to authentically express themselves is poor guidance because effective leadership requires strong filters and a primary focus on the audience's needs.

clips.hook: Eliminating distraction by focusing on one class at a time
clips.text: Immersive teaching formats allow professors to dedicate their entire professional focus to a single group of students without external distractions.

beschreibung:
The way leaders communicate can have a big impact on how we see ourselves. Vanessa Beasley is an expert on presidential rhetoric—and the president of Trinity University in San Antonio. In this episode, Adam and Vanessa take a closer look at how rhetoric used by past US presidents has shaped the identity of the American people, and explore some common rhetorical mistakes that leaders make when trying to persuade their audience. They also discuss why so many students are booing commencement speeches on AI, whether listening skills are declining, and how we can improve critical thinking on college campuses.
